Find peaks

Source: R/fit_peaks.R
find_peaks.Rd

Detects peaks in a chromatographic profile by finding zero-crossings in the smoothed first derivative of the signal (y). Smoothing suppresses spurious local extrema. Peaks can be filtered by minimum curvature (min_curvature), minimum amplitude (min_amplitude), or minimum prominence relative to the baseline noise (min_prominence_snr).

Usage

find_peaks(
  y,
  smooth_type = c("gaussian", "box", "savgol", "mva", "tmva", "none"),
  smooth_window = 3,
  min_curvature = 0,
  min_amplitude = 0,
  min_prominence_snr = 0,
  bounds = TRUE,
  slope_thresh = NULL,
  amp_thresh = NULL
)

Arguments

y

A chromatographic signal (as a numeric vector).

smooth_type

Type of smoothing. Either gaussian kernel ("gaussian"), box kernel ("box"), Savitzky-Golay smoothing ("savgol"), moving average ("mva"), triangular moving average ("tmva"), or no smoothing ("none").

smooth_window

Width of the smoothing window. A value between 0 and 1 is interpreted as a proportion of the length of y; a value of 1 or greater as a number of timepoints. Defaults to 3. See Choosing the smoothing window.

min_curvature

Minimum curvature at the apex, as the magnitude of the second derivative of the smoothed signal. Curvature scales as height over width squared, so larger values exclude broader peaks. Defaults to 0.

min_amplitude

Minimum peak amplitude, as the intensity of the unsmoothed signal at the apex. Apices at or below this value are removed. Defaults to 0, which removes apices at or below zero.

min_prominence_snr

Minimum peak prominence, as a multiple of the noise standard deviation. Requires bounds = TRUE. Only meaningful on baseline-corrected data (see Filtering peaks). Defaults to 0, which applies no filtering.

bounds

Logical. If TRUE (default), includes peak boundaries in a data.frame.

slope_thresh

The slope_thresh argument is deprecated. Please use min_curvature instead.

amp_thresh

The amp_thresh argument is deprecated. Please use min_amplitude instead.

Value

If bounds == TRUE, a data.frame with one row per peak and columns pos (apex), lower and upper (boundaries), and prominence. Otherwise, a numeric vector of apex positions. All locations are expressed as indices.

Details

How many peaks are detected depends mostly on smooth_window (see Choosing the smoothing window). Three filters, min_curvature, min_amplitude and min_prominence_snr, can then remove small or spurious peaks (see Filtering peaks).

Note

The find_peaks function is adapted from MATLAB code included in Prof. Tom O'Haver's Pragmatic Introduction to Signal Processing.

Choosing the smoothing window

Peaks are detected where the first derivative of the signal changes from positive to negative. Noise makes the derivative change sign many times on its own, so the signal is first smoothed over a window set by the smooth_window argument. A wider window suppresses more noise, but can also blur neighboring peaks together if the window is too wide.

Set smooth_window to about a third of the full width at half maximum of a typical peak, in timepoints. The default, 3, suits peaks about 10 timepoints wide. Wider windows may merge neighboring peaks. This may be easy to miss through casual inspection of peak tables — a merged pair is reported as one peak, with a single retention time and their combined area. Plot the peak list over the trace to check. Narrower windows add spurious apices. At fine time resolution, you can also reduce the resolution with the dim1 argument to preprocess.

A smooth_window between 0 and 1 is interpreted as a proportion of the run. A proportional smoothing window is invariant to sampling rate, but it scales with run length: 0.001 is only 3 timepoints for a 3,000-point trace but 100 for a 100,000-point one. A width supplied in timepoints has the opposite trade-off: it doesn't depend on run length, but it scales with the sampling rate, so if you change the time grid with preprocess(dim1 = ), the smooth_window should be scaled accordingly.

Under-smoothing also undermines min_prominence_snr. It can split a small peak into two apices, each measured from the shallow valley between them, so the filter discards both as noise and the peak is lost. Set the smoothing window wide enough to avoid splitting peaks before applying prominence filtering. find_peaks warns when smooth_window is under a third of the typical peak width.

The peak-finding article tests these recommendations on simulated chromatograms with known peaks.

Method-specific caveats. At the same smooth_window, "savgol" smooths about a third as much as the other methods, so it needs a wider window for the same noise reduction. It errors below 7 timepoints. "savgol", "mva", and "tmva" round the window to the nearest integer, then up to the next odd one if it is even. The moving averages also use at least three points, since a one-point window does no smoothing.

Filtering peaks

The curvature and amplitude filters (min_curvature and min_amplitude) are in absolute instrument units, so a usable value must be chosen for each dataset. The prominence filter (min_prominence_snr) instead measures each peak against the noise. A peak's prominence is its height above the higher of the two valleys on either side of it. For an isolated peak this is its full height; when a neighboring peak raises one of the valleys, it is less. The noise is estimated iteratively across the whole chromatogram. Starting with a rough estimate from the change in signal between adjacent timepoints, find_peaks excludes every peak whose apex is more than three times the current estimate above the median of the remaining timepoints, then re-estimates the noise as the scaled median absolute deviation of the remaining timepoints. This process is repeated until the estimate changes by less than 0.5%. min_prominence_snr = 4 keeps peaks with prominence exceeding 4x the estimated noise standard deviation.

Because the remaining timepoints include baseline drift, the estimated standard deviation can reflect drift rather than noise, so min_prominence_snr is only meaningful on baseline-corrected data.

References

O'Haver, Tom. Pragmatic Introduction to Signal Processing: Applications in scientific measurement. https://terpconnect.umd.edu/~toh/spectrum/ (Accessed January, 2022).
